tests.title: The Enhanced Games: rules and reactions

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Informal name for using performance-enhancing drugs in sport: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The opening explanation gives doping as the informal term for this use of drugs.

questions.prompt: City hosting the competition: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The reporter places the competition in Las Vegas, Nevada.

questions.prompt: Main sporting aim: to break {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The reporter identifies breaking world records as the event's aim.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What is different about the rules at these Games?

evidence.summary: These Games allow performance-enhancing drugs prohibited elsewhere in professional sport.

distractors.B: The programme describes the opposite relationship between the rules.
distractors.C: The description includes former Olympians and gives no such restriction.

options.label: A
options.text: They allow drugs that professional sports ban.

options.label: B
options.text: They ban drugs that professional sports allow.

options.label: C
options.text: They limit drug use to competitors without Olympic experience.

questions.prompt: Why would Neil not enjoy watching?

evidence.summary: Neil's initial objection centres on athletes starting and competing on an equal basis.

distractors.A: His objection is about fairness, not the competitors' Olympic experience.
distractors.B: The number of sports is mentioned earlier but is not his reason.

options.label: A
options.text: He prefers events without former Olympic competitors.

options.label: B
options.text: He thinks the programme offers too few sports.

options.label: C
options.text: He thinks the athletes should compete from the same level.

questions.prompt: What has the World Anti-Doping Agency spent decades doing?

evidence.summary: The Agency's longstanding opposition explains why the new event is controversial.

distractors.A: The three-event programme belongs to the new competition, not the Agency.
distractors.C: The Agency is described as fighting drug use, not organising these Games.

options.label: A
options.text: Choosing the three sports for the new Games.

options.label: B
options.text: Fighting the use of performance-enhancing drugs.

options.label: C
options.text: Organising supervised competitions for drug users.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Competitors may take the drugs under {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Dan Roan specifies medical supervision as a condition at the Games.

questions.prompt: The organisers compare open drug use with drugs taken {{blank}} elsewhere.

evidence.summary: Their safety comparison contrasts supervised open use with secret use at other competitions.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: Besides sporting integrity, what do critics say could be endangered? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Critics also warn about danger to the health of participants.

questions.prompt: What verb describes treating a previously unacceptable practice as acceptable? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The later explanation uses normalise for making a formerly unacceptable practice seem normal.

sourceReview.method: Official BBC transcript meaning cross-checked with the direct lesson recording; word-timed ASR used only to locate passages.

tests.title: Competing arguments: rules, safety and influence

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why is Armstrong introduced before the new competition?

evidence.summary: Armstrong's expulsion provides a contrast with a competition that permits performance-enhancing drugs.

distractors.B: The programme connects his exclusion, not Olympic participation, with drug rules.
distractors.C: His results do not establish how drugs are supervised elsewhere.

options.label: A
options.text: His exclusion illustrates the usual consequences of using banned substances.

options.label: B
options.text: His Olympic experience explains why the new Games have three events.

options.label: C
options.text: His race results establish that drug use is medically supervised everywhere.

questions.prompt: How does the reporter limit the comparison with the Olympics?

evidence.summary: The Olympic comparison is immediately narrowed to swimming, sprinting and weightlifting.

distractors.A: Some competitors are former Olympians, but no exclusive entry rule is stated.
distractors.B: The aim is to break world records, not solely Olympic records.

options.label: A
options.text: Only athletes who have won Olympic medals may enter.

options.label: B
options.text: Only Olympic records count towards the new event's aim.

options.label: C
options.text: Only three sports are included in the new competition.

questions.prompt: How do the presenters' initial reactions differ?

evidence.summary: Neil's fairness objection contrasts with Pippa's limited interest in watching sport.

distractors.A: Pippa mentions watching little sport, and Neil does not welcome drug use.
distractors.C: Medical supervision is discussed later and neither presenter makes that joint claim here.

options.label: A
options.text: Pippa objects to the event's limited programme, while Neil welcomes it.

options.label: B
options.text: Neil focuses on equal competition, while Pippa says she might not notice the difference.

options.label: C
options.text: Both initially argue that medical supervision resolves the fairness issue.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Length of the anti-doping campaign described: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The programme emphasises that opposition to performance-enhancing drugs has continued for decades.

questions.prompt: Condition attached to permitted drug-taking at the Games: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The permission described is linked to medical supervision rather than unrestricted private use.

questions.prompt: Country whose drug regulator the organisers cite: the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The organisers cite approval by a regulator in the United States, called the US in the recording.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What kind of line do critics say the event crosses? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The critics frame the boundary being crossed as ethical rather than merely sporting procedure.

questions.prompt: What quality of sport do critics say could be damaged? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Their objection includes potential harm to the integrity of sport.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: The concern about normalisation is that doping may come to seem {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Normalisation is explained as changing how acceptable or normal a practice seems.

questions.prompt: Because both sides hold strong arguments, the debate is far from {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The programme explicitly presents the disagreement as unresolved.

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

evidence.summary: Armstrong's removal is linked to using substances prohibited by the sport.

questions.prompt: In which US state is the host city located? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The report locates Las Vegas within Nevada.

questions.prompt: Which strength-based sport completes the list after swimming and sprinting? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Weightlifting is the third sport in the restricted programme.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: The permitted substances include steroids, growth hormones and {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Stimulants complete the list of substances allowed at the Games.

questions.prompt: Neil wants competitors to start from the same {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: His initial reaction makes a common starting level central to fair competition.

questions.prompt: The World Anti-Doping Agency's opposition has continued for {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The programme sets the new event against decades of anti-doping work.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What does Roan signal by introducing his assessment as fair to say?

evidence.summary: The phrase presents the assessment of controversy as balanced and reasonable.

distractors.A: The event is described as divisive, not as a settled issue.
distractors.C: The phrase introduces a judgement about controversy, not approval of the rules.

options.label: A
options.text: He regards the debate about the event as already settled.

options.label: B
options.text: He regards describing the event as controversial as a reasonable judgement.

options.label: C
options.text: He regards the rules of the competition as fair to every athlete.

questions.prompt: What is the organisers' safety comparison?

evidence.summary: The organisers compare supervised openness with clandestine drug use at other competitions.

distractors.B: The comparison is between ways of taking drugs, not drugs versus no drugs.
distractors.C: Approval is part of their argument but no claim that sporting rules are unnecessary is made.

options.label: A
options.text: Open use with supervision is safer than secret use elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Drug-taking is safer than competing without drugs.

options.label: C
options.text: Regulatory approval makes all sporting rules unnecessary.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: State of the dispute after both cases are presented: far from {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The presenter says the strongly held arguments leave the debate unresolved.

questions.prompt: Principle Neil still believes is missing: being {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Neil retains his fairness objection after hearing both sides.

tests.title: Fairness and risk: evaluating qualified claims

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Informal term for prohibited pharmacological enhancement in sport: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The opening defines doping through the use of performance-enhancing drugs in sport.

questions.prompt: Location of the new international competition: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The report identifies Las Vegas as the destination for participating athletes.

questions.prompt: Performance benchmark the organisers aim to exceed: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The aim is framed in terms of surpassing world records rather than simply winning medals.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by the presenters' first exchange?

evidence.summary: The exchange distinguishes Neil's principle of equal competition from Pippa's likely perception as a casual viewer.

distractors.B: Pippa describes her own viewing habits, not evidence about the drugs' effects.
distractors.C: The restricted programme is not their stated basis for assessing fairness.

options.label: A
options.text: Neil's objection concerns a shared competitive starting point, not how noticeable the drugs are to a casual viewer.

options.label: B
options.text: Pippa's limited viewing proves that the drugs cannot affect sporting performance.

options.label: C
options.text: Both speakers conclude that the choice of three sports creates the fairness problem.

questions.prompt: Which reading of Roan's opening phrase confuses its function with the subject matter?

evidence.summary: Fair to say qualifies the reasonableness of his statement and does not endorse the fairness of the Games.

distractors.A: The explanation explicitly links the phrase to a balanced assessment of controversy.
distractors.B: Calling the event divisive is consistent with that assessment, not the mistaken reading asked for.

options.label: A
options.text: He is presenting his description of the controversy as a reasonable assessment.

options.label: B
options.text: He is signalling confidence that calling the event divisive is justified.

options.label: C
options.text: He is declaring the drug rules themselves fair to competitors.

questions.prompt: Which claim stays within the organisers' stated comparison?

evidence.summary: The organisers' case concerns relative safety between open and secret drug use.

distractors.A: The argument addresses supervision and openness, not proof of equal starting conditions.
distractors.C: The organisers make a relative-safety claim, not a claim of zero risk.

options.label: A
options.text: Supervision demonstrates that enhanced and unenhanced competitors start equally.

options.label: B
options.text: Supervised, open use may be safer than taking the drugs secretly at other events.

options.label: C
options.text: Approval by the regulator establishes that taking drugs is risk-free.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: The explanation treats crossing the line as behaviour that is not socially {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The explanation locates the ethical boundary in what society accepts.

questions.prompt: Setting a bad example can encourage {{blank}} to behave badly too.

evidence.summary: The explanation connects an individual's or event's example with other people's conduct.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: What single word captures the principle Neil still finds absent after hearing the arguments? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Neil's final response retains fairness as the decisive issue for him.

questions.prompt: What word establishes that the reported victories formed an uninterrupted sequence? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The concluding account explicitly characterises the victories as consecutive.

tests.title: Doping debate: scope, attribution and implications

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Armstrong's exclusion followed his use of {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The introduction attributes Armstrong's removal to the use of prohibited substances.

questions.prompt: The comparison with the Olympics is restricted to swimming, sprinting and {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The report limits the event programme to three named sports, ending with weightlifting.

questions.prompt: Former medallists are described as pursuing financial rewards and {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The report distinguishes the pursuit of glory from the financial incentive.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What two-word type of substance is listed between steroids and stimulants? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Growth hormones occur between steroids and stimulants in the permitted-substance list.

questions.prompt: What does Neil say all athletes should start and compete from? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Neil describes fairness in terms of starting and competing from the same level.

questions.prompt: How long have anti-doping organisations been fighting these drugs, according to the programme? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The programme emphasises the decades-long campaign against performance-enhancing drugs.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Safeguard attached to drug use in Roan's description: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Roan describes permitted use as taking place under medical supervision.

questions.prompt: National origin of the regulator cited as approving the drugs: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The claimed approval is attributed to the regulator in the US.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What would overstate the organisers' argument?

evidence.summary: A relative-safety comparison does not amount to a claim that every health risk disappears.

distractors.B: They explicitly favour openly supervised use, so this does not overstate their argument.
distractors.C: Their claim is comparative, which is precisely the limit that the question asks listeners to notice.

options.label: A
options.text: That their arrangements eliminate every health risk associated with the drugs.

options.label: B
options.text: That they favour supervised openness over secret use.

options.label: C
options.text: That they regard their arrangements as comparatively safer.

questions.prompt: What links the critics' concern about example-setting to sporting integrity?

evidence.summary: The critics view normalisation as a precedent that could damage sporting integrity.

distractors.A: The earlier credentials of some athletes do not answer the critics' ethical concern.
distractors.B: The critics continue to raise ethics despite the organisers' approval argument.

options.label: A
options.text: Former Olympic medallists automatically preserve those standards.

options.label: B
options.text: Regulatory drug approval removes the need to assess ethical effects.

options.label: C
options.text: Normalising the practice may undermine standards beyond the immediate event.
